title: Trip Creation, Custody, and Completion
how_it_works_companion: How It Works chapter 10, section HOW TRIPS ARE RECORDED

sections.business_context:
A reservation is a promise about the future. A trip is what actually happened. When a member drives
away, the reservation’s job is done and the trip takes over: when the car really left, who really had it,
how far it really went, and what state it came back in.
This guide covers the trip record from checkout to check-in, the split between the shared trip facts and
the member-specific ones, and the odometer readings that anchor everything measured in miles.
The structural decision worth understanding: a trip has a core record shared by every kind of use, and
a companion record for the kind it is. A member trip and a service run are both trips, and only one of
them has points and a package.
Pairs with How It Works chapter 10, section HOW TRIPS ARE RECORDED.
sections.schema_overview:
TABLES USED BY THIS GUIDE

Table                             Role in this guide

VEHICLE_TRIP                      The core record: when, which car, how far, what fuel.

VEHICLE_TRIP_MEMBER               The member companion: package, participant, points, and snapshots.

VEHICLE_TRIP_SERVICE              The service companion: vendor, category, cost, and billing.

VEHICLE_ODOMETER_LOG              Every reading captured, whatever workflow captured it.

VEHICLE_EVENT_LOG                 Checkout, check-in, refuel, and damage events.

VEHICLE_RESERVATION               The reservation the trip came from.




KEY COLUMNS ON VEHICLE_TRIP

Column                            Purpose

vehicle_reservation_id            The booking this trip fulfills.

                                  Fk to VEHICLE_TRIP_TYPE_SELECT. Member, service, internal or event - and
trip_type_code                    the type decides whether the trip counts toward revenue and utilization and
                                  whether it posts member points.

start_time_actual,
                                  When the car really left and really came back.
end_time_actual

odometer_start_id,
                                  The two readings that bound the trip.
odometer_end_id

miles_driven                      The difference between them.

fuel_start_percent,
                                  Fuel out and fuel back.
fuel_end_percent

extra_miles, extra_miles_reason   Miles the club added and why: fuel, service, delivery.
sections.implementation_workflow:
1) Opening a Trip at Checkout
    1. Create the VEHICLE_TRIP row when the car actually leaves, not when the reservation said it
       would.
    2. Set trip_type_code from VEHICLE_TRIP_TYPE_SELECT. The type is not a label - it carries
       is_revenue and posts_points, which decide whether the trip counts toward revenue and
       utilization and whether it posts member points.
    3. Read those two flags rather than inferring behavior from the type name. A service trip posts no
       points because the row says so, not because the code recognizes the word service. That is
       what lets the club add a trip type as a row rather than as a release.
    4. Capture fuel_start_percent using VEHICLE_FUEL_LEVEL_SELECT. Staff pick a familiar
       fraction from a dropdown - Full, 7/8, 3/4 - and the platform stores the percent. Nothing holds a
       foreign key to that table by design; it converts on the way in so the stored values arithmetic
       cleanly for markup and consumption.
    5. Capture start_time_actual as the real moment. A member collecting two hours late has a trip
       that started two hours late, and the record should say so.
    6. Capture the starting odometer reading into VEHICLE_ODOMETER_LOG and point
       odometer_start_id at it.
    7. Record the checkout event in VEHICLE_EVENT_LOG and link it back to the reservation.
    8. Change the vehicle status to reflect that the car is out. See the Vehicles chapter.
    9. Create the companion record for the trip type in the same transaction.

2) Creating the Member Companion
    1. Capture member_id, member_package_id, and member_package_participant_id. All three
       matter: who, which membership, and which person on it.
    2. The package decides pricing and entitlement; the participant decides attribution and, on a split
       package, whose share is drawn.
    3. Capture branch_id, the branch the trip ran from, and the source that produced it.
    4. Capture start_type and return_type: whether the member collected the car or it was delivered,
       and whether they return it or the club collects.
    5. Snapshot the pricing at checkout: the vehicle tier, the weekday and weekend point values, the
       extra-mile value, and the included miles. These come from the package’s rate card and are
       frozen here.
    6. The snapshot is what makes a settled trip explainable years later. Without it the trip would
       have to be repriced against a card that may since have changed.

3) Custody During the Trip
    1. The member’s clock runs showroom to showroom. That single rule decides who pays for what,
       and everything below follows from it.
    2. Custody is tracked through handoff inspections, and every transfer captures an odometer
       reading. A handoff marks where staff driving ends and member driving begins; it does not
       mark where charging starts.
    3. Delivery: a checkout inspection captures condition and odometer as the car leaves the
       showroom, and a handoff inspection marks the moment the member receives it. The delivery
       leg rides on the member’s tab as staff-driven miles.
    4. Pickup: a single handoff inspection captures condition and odometer as the keys change
       hands at the showroom. There is no leg before it.
    5. Return: a handoff inspection captures the odometer when custody transfers back to staff,
       closing the member’s driving segment. If the car needs fuel, staff DRIVE it to refuel after the
       handoff, and the full check-in inspection at the showroom captures the final odometer and
       condition.
    6. Collection: a handoff inspection when the member surrenders the vehicle, and a check-in
       inspection when it arrives back at the showroom. The collection leg lands on the member’s tab
       the same way the delivery leg does.
    7. Every one of these moments is also logged as an event on the vehicle with photographs
       attached where they matter. See the Vehicle Inspections chapter.
    8. The trip is open. The car is with the member and the reservation is behind it.
    9. Events during the trip attach to it: a refuel, a damage report, a roadside incident. Each writes a
       VEHICLE_EVENT_LOG row against the trip.
    10. Set incident_flag on the member companion where something happened that needs following
        up. It is a signal, not a description; the events carry the detail.
    11. A trip cannot be edited into a different reservation. If the wrong booking was checked out, the
        trip is voided and reopened correctly rather than repointed.
    12. Every completed reservation produces exactly one trip, and the trip’s type mirrors the
        reservation that created it: a member trip, a service trip, a transport, or an internal use.

4) Closing a Trip at Check-In
    1. Capture end_time_actual, the closing odometer reading, and fuel_end_percent.
    2. Compute miles_driven from the two odometer readings, not from anything the member
       reports.
    3. Record extra_miles where STAFF drove the car during this member’s trip: the fuel run after a
       return, the repositioning miles of a delivery or a collection, or a service errand. Record the
       reason on each.
    4. Those miles are the member’s responsibility. The member did not drive them, but the
       member’s trip caused them, and the showroom-to-showroom rule puts them on the member’s
       tab. extra_miles records and explains them; it does not subtract them.
    5. miles_member is therefore the whole showroom-to-showroom figure, which is what
       miles_driven already measures. The only thing that reduces it is miles_member_adjustment.
    6. The one exception is miles the club drove for reasons that are not this member’s trip - a
       branch transfer, a service visit. Those are separate trips with their own records, not extra miles
       on a member trip.
    7. Record the check-in event and change the vehicle status. An inspection follows. See the
       Inspections chapter.
    8. The trip’s book does not close at the inspection desk. If the car still needs fuel, staff make that
       run and the miles are recorded against the trip. The car then goes on to be washed and
       detailed, where damage or a missing item that check-in did not catch can still be discovered,
       reported against the trip, and turned into tasks, charges, or flags for follow-up.
    9. The trip’s operational file accepts the whole wrap-up; it is settlement that finally closes the
       money. Do not close the trip record at check-in.
    10. Settlement follows check-in and is specified in the next guide.

EXAMPLE — WHOSE MILES ARE WHOSE

Reading                       Value             Meaning

Odometer at checkout          41,208            Anchors the start

Odometer at check-in          41,560            Anchors the end

                                                The difference; never member-reported. Showroom to
miles_driven                  352
                                                showroom.

                                                Of those 352, staff drove 40 - the delivery leg and the fuel
extra_miles                   40
                                                run. Recorded and explained, not subtracted.

miles_member_adjustment       0                 Nothing given back on this trip.

                                                The member is measured against the whole showroom-to-
miles_member                  352
                                                showroom figure.



5) The Three Numbers, and Why They Are Separate
    1. Member-driven miles: the odometer difference across the member’s own custody segment,
       handoff to handoff. This is operational truth and is never adjusted after the fact.
    2. Staff miles on the member’s tab: extra_miles, each with its reason. The member did not drive
       them; the member’s trip caused them.
    3. The goodwill reduction: miles_member_adjustment, always with a reason - a gesture, a
       dispute resolved in the member’s favor, an operational error corrected.
    4. Add the three together and the member’s total is the showroom-to-showroom story: every mile
       from the moment the car left until the moment it came home, less anything the club chose to
       give back.
    5. The design principle: what happened to the car is never rewritten, while what the member is
       billed can be adjusted - with an audit trail that always explains the difference.
    6. Where the club needs to adjust what a member is charged for, use miles_member_adjustment
       with a reason rather than editing miles_member.
    7. The adjustment is visible and explicable. An edited figure is neither.
    8. Adjustments happen: a faulty odometer, a member sent on a detour by a closure, a goodwill
       decision. All three deserve a record.

6) Odometer Readings
    1. Every reading goes into VEHICLE_ODOMETER_LOG, whatever workflow captured it:
       checkout, check-in, an inspection, a service visit.
    2. Record who captured it and when, and whether it was estimated.
    3. quality_flag distinguishes a Good reading from an Estimated, Corrected, or Invalid one. An
       Invalid reading is not silently accepted and must not be used in any mileage calculation.
    4. effective_at is when the reading was true, which may differ from when it was entered.
    5. The log is the vehicle’s mileage history and is what any question about total mileage should
       read, rather than a running column on the vehicle.
sections.rules_and_constraints:
1. A trip records what actually happened, not what the reservation said would happen.
    2. Every trip has a core record and exactly one companion for its type.
    3. A member trip records the member, the package, and the participant.
    4. Pricing is snapshotted at checkout from the package’s rate card, resolved through
       MEMBER_PACKAGE_RATE - the package’s own dated pointer, effective on the trip date.
       Never resolve through the series link, which is only the seed.
    5. miles_driven is computed from odometer readings and is never member-reported.
    6. The member is charged showroom to showroom: the delivery leg, the collection leg, and the
       fuel run are all the member’s responsibility.
    7. extra_miles records and explains the staff-driven portion of a member trip; it never subtracts
       from what the member is measured against.
    8. Member-driven miles are operational truth and are never adjusted after the fact.
    9. Only miles_member_adjustment reduces what the member is charged for, and it always
       carries a reason.
    10. Every completed reservation produces exactly one trip, whose type mirrors the reservation.
    11. The trip’s operational file stays open past check-in; settlement is what closes it.
    12. Member miles are adjusted through miles_member_adjustment with a reason, never by
        editing.
    13. A trip is never repointed to a different reservation.
    14. Every odometer reading is logged with its capturer, its quality, and when it was true.
sections.integration_and_edge_cases:
1. A member collecting late. The trip starts when the car leaves. The reservation window is
       what was promised; the trip is what happened, and settlement uses the trip.
    2. A car delivered rather than collected. The trip still starts when the car leaves the branch,
       and the delivery miles are extra_miles rather than the member’s.
    3. A member returning early. The trip ends when the car comes back. For a weekend, the
       bundled rate still applies in full; see the Membership Plans chapter.
    4. An odometer that has been replaced. The readings jump. quality_flag and a corrected
       reading are how that is handled, rather than pretending the car did negative miles.
    5. A trip with no reservation. Should not happen for a member trip and does happen for
       internal moves. The reservation link is nullable for that reason.
    6. The wrong car checked out. Void the trip and open the correct one. Repointing would make
       the odometer readings belong to a car that never moved.
    7. A trip open for weeks. A car out for extended service. Legitimate, and the reason nothing
       assumes a trip is short.
    8. A member trip on a shared package. The participant is who drove; the package is whose
       allowance is drawn. On a split package those two together decide whose share is used.
sections.automations_and_notifications:
Each automation below is listed with its trigger and its expected outcome. Operational specification is
reserved for the automations pass that follows the first draft of all chapters.

AUTOMATIONS IN THIS GUIDE

Trigger                           Outcome

Checkout recorded                 Trip opened; pricing snapshotted; vehicle status changed; event logged.

Check-in recorded                 Trip closed; miles computed; inspection raised; settlement begins.

Implausible odometer reading      Flagged for review rather than accepted.

Incident flagged during a trip    Task raised for follow-up.

Trip open past its expected end   Surfaced to the branch.



Reserved for the automations pass: how far past an expected end a trip is surfaced, what makes an
odometer reading implausible, and who receives incident follow-ups.
sections.developer_notes:
1. Actual, not scheduled. Every time on the trip is what happened. Copying the reservation
       times into the trip loses the only reason the trip exists as a separate record.
    2. Snapshot at checkout. Tier, point values, extra-mile rate, and included miles. Settlement
       reads the snapshot, not the card, so a card change can never reprice a completed trip.
    3. Miles come from the odometer. Two readings, one subtraction. Any member-reported figure
       is a claim, not a measurement.
    4. Extra miles are the club’s. Delivery, fuel runs, and service moves all put miles on the car that
       the member did not drive. Charging them is the most avoidable complaint in the chapter.
    5. Adjust, never edit. miles_member_adjustment with a reason. An edited mileage figure cannot
       be explained to a member six months later.
    6. One companion per trip type. The core record carries what every trip shares; the companion
       carries what only that kind has. A single wide table would leave most columns empty most of
       the time.
    7. Void and reopen, never repoint. A trip belongs to the reservation it was opened against.
